title: The Billable Hour is Dead; Long Live the Billable Hour — Kevin Madura + Mo Bhasin, Alix Partners

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: Two of three detailed use cases center on structured outputs and structured generation for vendor categorization and document extraction, with log-prob confidence scoring as a key technical contribution. The talk describes an internal enterprise GenAI platform at a global consulting firm automating knowledge-work workflows and enterprise RAG over corporate document corpora. The talk covers building the platform over two years, deploying 50 production instances, and evaluating via accuracy metrics and confidence scoring. The talk mixes accessible business framing with practical implementation details such as structured output schemas, API embedding, and geometric mean log-prob confidence. Conference talk at AI Engineer World's Fair presenting enterprise war stories with code examples and three deployed use cases. All quantitative claims and use case descriptions are sourced directly from the transcript with specific excerpts.

summary: Mo Bhasin (Director of AI Products) and Kevin Madura from AlixPartners, a global management consulting firm, share lessons from building an internal GenAI platform over two years with 20 engineers, 50 deployments, and hundreds of users. They frame the talk around three themes: how AI reshapes knowledge work, three real deployment use cases, and what doesn't work plus future directions. They contrast the junior leverage model (many junior staff directed by seniors) with AlixPartners' senior leverage model (experienced practitioners doing the work), predicting a hybrid future where AI replicates senior expertise at scale. They describe three engagement phases—data ingestion/normalization, analysis/hypothesis generation, and deliverables—showing AI compresses the first phase from ~50% to 10-20% of effort while enabling 100% data coverage instead of top-20% prioritization. They highlight the investment paradox: 89% of CEOs plan AI, but NBER, BCG, and S&P Global report minimal realized enterprise value, attributing this to conflating employee productivity with enterprise productivity. Use Case 1 (Categorization): structured outputs replace traditional ML pipelines, achieving 95% accuracy on 10,000 vendors in minutes vs. days at order-of-magnitude less cost. Use Case 2 (Enterprise RAG): handling hundreds of gigabytes across formats, replacing manual indices and SharePoint search. They taught LLMs to call third-party proprietary database APIs, democratizing access that previously took days. RAG serves as a substrate for additional GenAI features, though user expectations exceed current capabilities—"reason across all documents" is not how RAG works. Use Case 3 (Structured Extraction): combining documents with schemas, LLMs, and validation to extract structured data from unstructured sources like 50-page credit agreements. The schema's flexibility enables reuse across engagement types. At scale, thousands to hundreds of thousands of documents are processed in minutes vs. days or weeks of human review. For user trust, they use OpenAI API log probs aligned with structured output schemas—taking the geometric mean of log probs for extracted values as a confidence proxy, displayed via green/yellow visual indicators. Key scaling requirements include monthly demos (prototyping in Streamlit, building in React), NPS/ROI as primary metrics earned one bug fix at a time, and partnerships as a shared journey.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Platform Overview
sections.summary: Mo Bhasin and Kevin Madura introduce themselves and AlixPartners, a global management consulting firm. They describe their internal GenAI platform built over two years with 20 engineers, 50 deployments, and hundreds of users. They outline three talk themes: AI reshaping knowledge work, three real use cases, and what doesn't work.

sections.title: AI Reshaping Knowledge Work and Professional Services Models
sections.summary: They reference METR charts showing LLM task-length capability takeoff, noting professional services disruption will be less steep due to messiness of real-world knowledge work. They contrast the junior leverage model with AlixPartners' senior leverage model. They predict a hybrid future referencing Dwarkesh Patel's AI-first firm concept where senior expertise is replicated at scale through AI.

sections.title: Three Engagement Phases and AI's Impact
sections.summary: They describe three engagement phases: upfront data ingestion/normalization/categorization, analysis and hypothesis generation, and client deliverables. AI compresses the first phase from ~50% to 10-20% of human effort. AI removes the human throughput bottleneck, enabling analysis of 100% of data corpora instead of prioritizing only the top 20%.

sections.title: The AI Investment Paradox
sections.summary: Mo introduces the paradox: 89% of CEOs plan AI implementation (Deloitte), but NBER finds no significant earnings/hours impact, BCG reports three-quarters of companies fail to scale value, and S&P Global says nearly half are abandoning AI initiatives. They attribute this to the difference between employee productivity and enterprise productivity.

sections.title: Use Case 1: Categorization with Structured Outputs
sections.summary: Mo presents categorization replacing traditional ML pipelines with LLM structured outputs and tool calls. Example: classifying vendors into NAICS taxonomy codes. Results: 95% accuracy on 10,000 vendors in minutes vs. days at order-of-magnitude less cost. Lessons: accuracy requires business partner collaboration, converts skeptics to champions, embeds business context in taxonomies, builds robust steps for future agentic workflows, and results are stochastic not deterministic.

sections.title: Use Case 2: Enterprise-Scale RAG
sections.summary: Mo presents enterprise-scale RAG handling hundreds of gigabytes across PowerPoint, Word, Excel, and CSV formats, replacing manual Excel indices and unreliable SharePoint search. Key innovation: teaching LLMs to call third-party proprietary database APIs by embedding API specs, democratizing access that previously took days through siloed web UI and email workflows. RAG serves as a substrate for additional GenAI features. Trade-off: user expectations exceed current capabilities—'reason across all documents' is not how RAG works; solutions must be built step by step.

sections.title: Use Case 3: Structured Data Extraction from Unstructured Data
sections.summary: Kevin presents structured extraction combining documents with schemas, LLMs, and validation scaffolding. Example: extracting contract parties, maturity date, and senior lenders from 50-page credit agreement PDFs. The schema's flexibility enables reuse across engagement types (investigations vs. M&A). Scales to hundreds of thousands of documents, reducing human review from days/weeks to minutes. For user trust, they use OpenAI API log probs aligned with structured output schemas—taking the geometric mean of log probs for extracted value tokens as a confidence proxy, displayed via green/yellow visual indicators for intuitive human review.

sections.title: Key Requirements for Scaling GenAI and Final Thoughts
sections.summary: Mo outlines must-haves for scaling: monthly demos (prototyping in Streamlit, building in React) to inspire the firm and sustain investment; NPS and ROI as primary metrics earned one bug fix at a time despite the lure of shiny new technologies like agents and MCP; and partnerships as a shared journey. He closes with a humorous note that once Excel-powered LLMs work, we will be at AGI.

demonstrations: Categorization use case: classifying 10,000 vendors into NAICS codes using structured outputs and web query tool calls
RAG use case: handling 80+ gigs of internal documents across PowerPoint, Word, Excel, CSV formats with API-taught LLM access to proprietary databases
Structured extraction use case: extracting contract parties, maturity date, senior lenders from 50-page credit agreement PDFs
Confidence visualization: green/yellow boxes reflecting log-prob-derived confidence levels on extracted values like LIBOR plus 1% per annum

Professional services disruption will be less steep than software engineering due to real-world messiness
